requirement: In a book chapter, each valid `{impl}`, `{cite}`, or `{test}` reference MUST render as a Shields.io static badge image with meaningful alt text that displays its role and full name and links to the badge at the corresponding `{req}` or `{example}` definition. Links MUST work across chapters, including nested chapters. Each fenced `{req}` or `{example}` directive MUST render as a Shields.io definition badge image identifying its kind; text outside a directive MUST remain literal. Badge text MUST remain legible regardless of whether its link has been visited. These badges use the syntax defined by {cite}`requirements.references.targets`.
rationale: The Rust implementation and tests cover the requirement well. The gap is the CSS file marked as `{impl}`, which carries behavior the requirement does not specify. **What is implemented and tested** - `replace_references` (src/lib.rs, line ~372) turns each valid `{impl}`, `{cite}` and `{test}` role into an `` wrapping a Shields.io ``. - The badge's alt text is "role full-name", built by `shield_badge`. - The link goes through `chapter_href` to the `habeas-req-` or `habeas-example-` anchor on the defining chapter. It uses `../` prefixes, so it works from nested chapters. - Unknown names are left literal. - `replace_definitions` (line ~278) renders each closed `{req}` or `{example}` directive as a definition badge whose kind is shown by `DefinitionKind::badge()`. Roles outside a directive stay literal. - `ReferenceKind::label` and `color` supply the role text and colour, and `DefinitionKind::anchor` supplies the anchor id. - `.habeas-req-badge`, `a.habeas-req-badge:visited { color: inherit; text-decoration: none }` and the related rules in `md/habeas.css` keep badges legible after a link is visited. - Tests: - `shields_badge_urls_escape_requirement_names` checks the URL and alt text. - `references_in_nested_chapters_link_to_the_requirement_definition` checks all three roles, their colours and a nested-chapter link. - `colon_directives_render_markdown_bodies_and_legacy_roles_stay_literal` checks that roles outside a directive stay literal. - `examples_are_distinct_definitions_and_tests_link_to_them` checks example badges and links. **Why this is a gap** - `md/habeas.css` is anchored whole with `:impl:` to `requirements.references.book_badges` (md/requirements/references.md, line 38). - Lines 27–53 of the file hold unrelated styling. It is a numbered-step layout for the project's intro page, selected by `#mdbook-content main > h1#habeas-codicem ~ ol:first-of-type`. It uses `counter-reset: intro-step`, large `::before` numerals and similar rules. - This is behavior in the `{impl}` code that the requirement does not specify, and I found no other requirement or example that covers it (searches for `intro-step` and `habeas-codicem` find only the CSS, the book's name and URLs). - The file is also embedded in `src/setup.rs` as `BADGE_CSS` and written into user projects, so the project-specific intro styling ships with the badge CSS. - The hover brightness and focus-outline rules are also unspecified, though they are minor. - No FIXME or issue reference acknowledges this gap. Because of the unspecified behavior in the whole-file CSS `{impl}` anchor, the requirement is not met exactly as stated.

- `{impl}`: the source implements part of the definition. It makes a decision, performs a check, produces an output, or handles a case the definition specifies. Calling code that implements a definition, or producing a result a caller uses to meet it, is not implementing it. A requirement that refines another requirement's obligation can `{impl}` it. A convention for every output of a kind, such as every validation error, is implemented by the code that carries it out as a whole.
- `{test}`: the source is designed to verify behavior the definition specifies, either a test through its scenario and assertions, or a named example through its concrete case.

Only requirements and examples are assessed; code is reviewed as part of the definitions it implements or tests. `{impl}` and `{test}` point from the definition to the source, so the source becomes a mandatory input to the definition's assessment, and that definition's evidence must cover the reference line. `{cite}` points from the source to the definition: a citing requirement or example receives the cited declaration as context, and the citing site needs no evidence coverage. Marking only `{cite}` on code that implements part of a requirement leaves a gap in that requirement's review. In the book, references and definitions become linked badges.

Some sources cannot or should not carry a reference themselves, such as a shipped agent skill. A requirement can anchor such a file with `:impl:` or `:test:` option lines immediately after its opening fence; an example can use `:test:`. Each anchor is an edge to the complete file, so that requirement's evidence must contain an input covering every line of it, and changing the file makes the evidence stale. Option lines are not part of the requirement text. Prefer a precise in-source reference whenever one is possible.
The bundled skill MUST explain how to author evidence.

`habeas info <selection>` MUST show the requirements and named examples matched by the {term}`requirements.references.definition_selection`. It MUST print matches in full-name order as Markdown with the same kind-labeled definition, Validation findings, Rationale, and Inputs structure and evidence states as mdBook detail pages, including readable output for missing or invalid evidence. It MUST work without a requirements index directive and report an invalid selection or no matches clearly. Habeas's bundled agent guidance MUST tell agents they can use this command to inspect a requirement or named example.

Habeas MUST bundle a skill for deriving initial requirements from an existing codebase. The skill MUST direct agents to read the code and tests, map every first-party test to at least one requirement or example, identify and map every source unit implementing end-user-visible functionality or interactions to a requirement, and report gaps rather than claim complete coverage without an independent inventory review.

The bundled requirements skill MUST direct agents adding or changing user-visible behavior in a Habeas project to draft stable requirement IDs and exact text, obtain the user's agreement, and install the agreed requirements in the mdBook before writing implementation or test code. It MUST direct agents to review substantive changes to agreed obligations with the user. The bootstrap skill MUST require user review of requirements inferred from existing code before installing them. The evidence skill MUST accept missing evidence or truthful false judgments from the harness while implementation is pending; it MUST NOT direct the supervising agent to write placeholder evidence itself.

Habeas's bundled agent skills MUST direct agents reviewing code against requirements to inspect every end-user-observable result and branch, including errors and input handling, and verify both that the code fulfills each applicable requirement and that it introduces no additional end-user-observable behavior without an agreed requirement. They MUST explain the requirement and example review criteria in {cite}`requirements.ci.review_criteria`, including test adequacy and justified absence of tests for requirements, and the three outcomes and documented-gap convention in {cite}`requirements.ci.outcomes`. Agents MUST mark code that implements part of a requirement with `{impl}` and tests that verify it with `{test}`, using `{cite}` only for related code that does neither, under {cite}`requirements.references.targets`. Where requirements interact, agents MUST mark every requirement implemented at the relevant point and explain how their texts jointly account for the behavior. A citation alone MUST NOT count as that explanation.

Habeas's bundled agent skills MUST NOT offer a waiver for an uncited first-party Rust function. When a function serves only as an internal implementation detail and no existing requirement explains it, Habeas's bundled agent skills MUST direct agents to propose an explicit project requirement scoped to one area of internal code, such as `internal.config_parsing`, rather than one catch-all requirement, obtain the user's agreement, mark the function with `{impl}`, and run `habeas author --all` for the harness to assess that requirement's evidence. That assessment MUST account for whether the requirement explains each implementing function's behavior. An internal-detail requirement MUST NOT justify an otherwise unspecified end-user-observable behavior.

Each evidence detail page MUST display its state as a Shields.io static badge image with meaningful alt text and the current requirement or example body as a Markdown block quote labeled by kind. It MUST render the recorded rationale as Markdown in a Rationale section and display the recorded FIXME strings when the determination is FIXME. Inputs MUST be grouped under headings in this order: Implementation, for sources reached by an `{impl}` edge from the definition, including anchored files; Tests, for sources reached by a `{test}` edge, including tests, examples, and anchored files; Referenced definitions, for declarations the definition cites and their terminology; and Other sources, for the remaining inputs the assessment consulted. Edges MUST be determined from the current references under {cite}`requirements.references.targets` and {cite}`requirements.references.anchors`. Each group and each input MUST be a collapsible disclosure element, with groups expanded and inputs collapsed by default, so readers can move between groups and open individual sources. Each input MUST have its own subsection identifying its selector. A file-range or Rust-item input MUST show its resolved file and inclusive line range. A requirements input MUST show its selection and each matched definition's full name, file, and inclusive line range. Each subsection MUST show the exact recorded text in a fenced code block. Code fences MUST request Rust highlighting for `.rs` files and language-aware highlighting for Markdown, JSON, TOML, Java, JavaScript, TypeScript, and Python files; TOML MAY use INI highlighting when native TOML highlighting is unavailable.
